lessons.title: Networking Foundations for the Exam
lessons.summary: OSI layers, CIDR, routing, BGP, MTU and how a VPC really forwards packets.
takeaways: Layer determines capability: L7 can read HTTP, L4 sees ports, L3 forwards packets.
A VPC subnet loses five addresses; overlapping CIDRs block peering and complicate routing.
Longest prefix always wins first; then static beats propagated, and BGP uses local preference and AS_PATH.
Blocked ICMP type 3 code 4 plus an MTU mismatch causes large transfers to hang while small ones succeed.
Security groups are stateful, network ACLs are stateless, and route tables choose the next hop.

title: Amazon CloudFront Design Patterns

source.caption: Protecting each origin type. Each layer removes the direct-to-origin path.

layers.title: S3 origin
layers.note: Origin access control (OAC): bucket policy allows only the CloudFront service principal for that distribution. Block public access stays on.

layers.title: ALB / NLB / EC2 in private subnets
layers.note: CloudFront VPC origins keep the origin private with no public IP, reached through a service-managed ENI.

layers.title: Public ALB or custom origin
layers.note: Allow the AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront origin-facing IPs in the security group, plus a secret custom header the origin verifies (rotate it).

layers.title: API Gateway
layers.note: Use an edge-optimized or regional endpoint with a CloudFront-added header or API key; resource policy or WAF for validation.

layers.title: Viewer side
layers.note: HTTPS only (redirect HTTP), TLS 1.2+ security policy, AWS WAF web ACL attached to the distribution.

title: Edge Networking and Global Traffic (Task 1.1)

lessons.title: Amazon CloudFront Design Patterns
lessons.summary: Origins, caching, security, private origins and integration with ALB, S3 and API Gateway.
takeaways: Edge location, regional edge cache, optional Origin Shield, then origin; keep the cache key minimal for a high hit ratio.
Use OAC for S3 and VPC origins or prefix list plus custom header for load balancer origins so CloudFront cannot be bypassed.
Origin groups give origin failover; signed URLs/cookies protect private content; field-level encryption protects specific fields.
WAF web ACLs and ACM certificates for CloudFront live in us-east-1.
CloudFront Functions for light viewer logic; Lambda@Edge for heavier or origin-side logic.

lessons.title: AWS Global Accelerator and Global Traffic Management
lessons.summary: Anycast IPs, endpoint groups, traffic dials and when to pick it over CloudFront.
takeaways: Global Accelerator provides two static anycast IPs and routes over the AWS backbone to healthy endpoints in the best Region.
Traffic dials work per endpoint group, weights per endpoint; health-check failover does not depend on DNS TTLs.
Choose CloudFront for caching and HTTP edge logic, Global Accelerator for TCP/UDP, static IPs and fast failover.
Custom routing accelerators map users to specific EC2 instances and ports.

title: DNS on AWS (Tasks 1.2, 2.3)

lessons.title: Route 53 Hosted Zones, Records and Registration
lessons.summary: Public and private zones, alias records, delegation and domain registration.
takeaways: Public zones serve the internet; private zones serve associated VPCs and require enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames.
Alias records work at the apex, are free for AWS targets and follow target changes; CNAMEs cannot be at the apex.
Cross-account PHZ association needs an authorization from the zone account and an association from the VPC account.
Delegation uses NS records in the parent zone; registrar name servers must match the hosting zone.

lessons.title: Route 53 Routing Policies and Health Checks
lessons.summary: Weighted, latency, failover, geolocation, geoproximity, IP-based and multivalue.
takeaways: Match policy to requirement: weighted for splits, latency for speed, geolocation for residency (with a default), geoproximity for biased distance, failover for DR, IP-based for client network mapping.
Health checkers are internet-based; monitor private resources through CloudWatch alarm health checks.
DNS failover time is detection plus TTL plus caching, so choose short TTLs for fast recovery.
Nest policies with alias records or Traffic Flow for multi-dimensional routing.

lessons.title: Hybrid and Multi-Account DNS with Resolver
lessons.summary: Inbound and outbound endpoints, forwarding rules, RAM sharing and Route 53 Profiles.
takeaways: The VPC resolver (VPC base + 2, 169.254.169.253) is not reachable externally; use inbound endpoints for on-premises-to-AWS queries.
Outbound endpoints plus forwarding rules send chosen domains to on-premises DNS; rules take precedence over PHZs.
Use two or more AZs per endpoint and allow port 53 TCP/UDP end to end.
Share forwarding rules with RAM, or bundle configuration with Route 53 Profiles, to manage DNS centrally.

lessons.title: DNSSEC, DNS Firewall and DNS Logging
lessons.summary: Sign zones, validate answers, block bad domains and log every query.
takeaways: DNSSEC gives authenticity and integrity through a chain of trust (DS in the parent), not confidentiality.
Route 53 DNSSEC signing: public zones only, asymmetric ECC_NIST_P256 KMS key in us-east-1, then add DS at the parent last.
Resolver DNSSEC validation protects VPC clients; DNS Firewall blocks bad domains and can fail open or closed.
Public zone query logs go to CloudWatch Logs in us-east-1; Resolver query logs go to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose.

title: Hybrid Connectivity (Tasks 1.5, 2.1)

lessons.title: AWS Direct Connect: Design and Resiliency
lessons.summary: Connection types, locations, LOA-CFA and the resiliency models.
takeaways: Direct Connect is a private, consistent, non-encrypted link through a colocation facility, requiring a cross connect (LOA-CFA).
Dedicated connections: 1, 10, 100 Gbps; hosted connections: 50 Mbps to 25 Gbps via partners with one VIF each.
Maximum resiliency (two locations, two devices each) is required for the 99.99% SLA; use BFD for fast failover.
Use VPN for quick start or low-cost backup; Direct Connect for steady high bandwidth and lower transfer cost.

lessons.title: Direct Connect: VIFs, Gateways and Layer 2 Details
lessons.summary: Private, public and transit VIFs, Direct Connect gateway, LAG, MACsec and MTU.
takeaways: Private VIFs reach VPCs, transit VIFs reach Transit Gateways, public VIFs reach AWS public endpoints only.
A Direct Connect gateway is global and connects one VIF to many VGWs (up to 20) or Transit Gateways (up to 3) but never routes between them.
LAG aggregates bandwidth at one location; MACsec encrypts layer 2; jumbo is 9001 on private VIFs and 8500 on transit VIFs.
Mind the 100-prefix limit on BGP sessions and validate with state, light-level metrics and Reachability Analyzer.

lessons.title: Site-to-Site VPN and Client VPN
lessons.summary: Tunnels, ECMP, accelerated VPN, private IP VPN and remote-user access.
takeaways: A Site-to-Site VPN connection has two tunnels in different AZs; configure both and prefer BGP for dynamic failover.
ECMP across tunnels and connections needs a Transit Gateway; a VGW does not support ECMP.
Accelerated VPN uses Global Accelerator and requires Transit Gateway; Private IP VPN runs over a Direct Connect transit VIF.
Client VPN offers certificate, AD and SAML authentication, authorization rules per CIDR, split tunnel and logging.

lessons.title: BGP Routing and Traffic Engineering
lessons.summary: Attributes, communities, prefix limits and active/passive versus load sharing.
takeaways: Longest prefix always wins before any BGP attribute; then local preference, AS_PATH, MED.
AWS honours Direct Connect local-preference communities 7224:7100/7200/7300 and public-VIF scope communities 7224:9100/9200/9300.
Direct Connect BGP beats VPN on a VGW; on a Transit Gateway static wins, then VPC, DXGW, Connect, VPN.
Keep paths symmetric for stateful firewalls and summarize prefixes to respect limits.

lessons.title: Redundant Hybrid Architectures and SD-WAN
lessons.summary: Combining Direct Connect and VPN, Transit Gateway Connect and GRE overlays.
takeaways: Layer redundancy: separate devices, locations and providers, with VPN as a cost-effective backup.
BGP makes failover automatic; keep symmetric preferences on both sides.
Transit Gateway Connect uses GRE with BGP over VPC or Direct Connect transport, with up to four peers and about 5 Gbps each.
GRE does not encrypt, IPsec does; VXLAN and GENEVE appear in mirroring and GWLB.

lessons.title: VPC Design, Addressing and Overlapping CIDRs
lessons.summary: Subnets, secondary CIDRs, IPv6, NAT gateways and overlap strategies.
takeaways: Use per-AZ NAT gateways and separate route tables per subnet tier.
Add secondary CIDRs (including 100.64.0.0/10), IPv6 or prefix delegation to avoid IP exhaustion; IPAM prevents overlaps.
For overlapping CIDRs, prefer PrivateLink for service access or a private NAT gateway for IP-level access.
Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB avoid NAT gateway data processing charges.

lessons.title: VPC Peering Compared with Transit Gateway
lessons.summary: Limits, transitivity, cost and the decision table.
takeaways: Peering is private, cheap, fast and non-transitive; CIDRs must not overlap and routes are needed on both sides.
Transit Gateway scales to thousands of attachments with route-table segmentation, at a per-attachment and per-GB cost.
PrivateLink exposes a service, not a network, and tolerates overlapping CIDRs.
Full mesh grows as n(n-1)/2; use hub-and-spoke past a few VPCs.

lessons.title: Transit Gateway Architectures
lessons.summary: Route tables, association and propagation, appliance mode, peering and multicast.
takeaways: Association chooses the table used for traffic from an attachment; propagation advertises an attachment's routes into tables.
Disable default association/propagation to segment prod, dev, shared and on-premises.
Appliance mode keeps flows symmetric across AZs for stateful inspection.
TGW peering uses static routes; share a TGW across accounts with RAM; multicast needs a multicast domain and Nitro instances.

lessons.title: AWS PrivateLink and VPC Endpoints
lessons.summary: Gateway and interface endpoints, endpoint services and endpoint policies.
takeaways: Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) are free route-based and local to the VPC; interface endpoints are ENIs reachable from on-premises and peers.
Publish a service with an NLB-backed endpoint service; connectivity is one-way and overlap-tolerant.
Control access with endpoint policies, bucket policies using aws:SourceVpce, and security groups.
Private DNS lets default service names resolve to endpoint ENIs inside the VPC.

lessons.title: VPC Sharing, Organizations and Resource Access Manager
lessons.summary: Share subnets, Transit Gateways and rules across accounts.
takeaways: VPC sharing lets participants deploy into owner-managed subnets; the owner controls routing, participants control their own resources.
RAM shares Transit Gateways, Resolver rules, prefix lists and more; use Organizations for organization-wide sharing.
Use AZ IDs, SCP guardrails, Control Tower and a dedicated network account for governance.
Choose VPC sharing for central control and cost; separate VPCs for autonomy and isolation.

lessons.title: Network Monitoring with CloudWatch
lessons.summary: Metrics, alarms, logs and baselines for each networking service.
takeaways: Start from requirements (who, how fast, what question, retention) and pick metrics and logs accordingly.
Know the signature metrics per service: VPN TunnelState, DX ConnectionState and light levels, NAT ErrorPortAllocation, ALB 5XX and target response time.
Composite alarms and anomaly detection reduce noise; missing data should be breaching for heartbeat-like metrics.
Capture baselines and read ENA allowance counters when drops have no other explanation.

lessons.title: VPC Flow Logs and Traffic Mirroring
lessons.summary: Fields, formats, destinations, limits and packet-level inspection.
takeaways: Flow logs capture metadata at VPC, subnet, ENI or Transit Gateway level and deliver to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose; configurations are immutable.
Use custom fields such as pkt-srcaddr, flow-direction and traffic-path for NAT and path analysis; know what is not logged.
Traffic Mirroring copies full packets over VXLAN UDP 4789 from Nitro ENIs to ENI, NLB or GWLB targets.
REJECT for return traffic with accepted request usually means a stateless NACL issue.

lessons.title: Reachability Analyzer, Network Manager and Route Analyzer
lessons.summary: Prove connectivity intent and map global topology.
takeaways: Reachability Analyzer models configuration without sending packets; it names the blocking component but cannot see OS firewalls or on-premises devices.
Route Analyzer checks only the TGW route table; Network Manager gives a global topology with metrics and events.
Network Access Analyzer finds unintended paths against a policy scope.
Automate Reachability Analyzer runs to continuously verify intended connectivity.

lessons.title: Network Automation and Infrastructure as Code
lessons.summary: CloudFormation, CDK, event-driven automation and avoiding hard-coded values.
takeaways: Use CloudFormation or CDK for repeatable, reviewable network stacks; StackSets scale them across accounts and Regions.
Avoid hard-coded AZs, CIDRs, IDs, Regions, account IDs and secrets; use parameters, GetAZs, Cidr, SSM and Secrets Manager.
EventBridge connects CloudTrail, Config, CloudWatch and Network Manager events to Lambda and SSM Automation for self-healing and guardrails.
Automate verification and cost cleanup, and keep on-premises and AWS configs generated from one source.

lessons.summary: Propagation, summarization, route priority and the limits that bite.
takeaways: Keep explicit route tables per subnet tier, use prefix lists and alert on blackhole routes.
Summarize aligned address blocks to respect prefix limits, but keep specifics for multi-homed or critical networks.
Know the order of magnitude of limits: 100 prefixes per VIF, 5,000 TGW attachments, 125 peerings, 5 SGs per ENI, 55,000 NAT connections.
Use the right pattern per scope: peering or TGW and PrivateLink within a Region; TGW peering, cross-Region peering and DX gateway across Regions.

lessons.title: Network Troubleshooting Playbook
lessons.summary: A layered method, MTU and MSS problems, asymmetric routing and common faults.
takeaways: Troubleshoot in layers: flow definition, DNS, routes, filters, path quality, application.
Symptom 'small works, large fails' means MTU/MSS with blocked ICMP type 3 code 4; clamp MSS and align MTUs.
No REJECT but no reply suggests routing or host issues; REJECT points to SG or NACL.
Asymmetric paths break stateful devices; align preferences and enable appliance mode.

lessons.title: Performance and Cost Optimization
lessons.summary: ENA, EFA, jumbo frames, multicast, data transfer costs and subnet planning.
takeaways: ENA is the default fast NIC; ENA Express lifts single flows to 25 Gbps in an AZ; EFA gives OS-bypass transport for HPC/ML inside a subnet.
Single flows are limited (about 5 Gbps, 10 Gbps in a cluster placement group), so parallelize.
Jumbo frames need the whole path; multicast needs Transit Gateway multicast domains and Nitro instances.
Gateway endpoints, AZ locality, CloudFront and peering cut data-transfer costs; secondary CIDRs fix subnet exhaustion.

lessons.title: Threat Modeling and Securing Inbound Traffic
lessons.summary: WAF, Shield, perimeter VPCs and three-tier designs.
takeaways: Model threats by trust boundary and data flow, then map each threat to a control.
Layer the inbound path: edge services, WAF and Shield, load balancer, private application and isolated data tiers.
WAF handles layer 7 on CloudFront, ALB and API Gateway; Shield Standard is free, Advanced adds response team and cost protection.
Isolate untrusted networks and compliance scopes in separate VPCs or accounts and test the controls.

lessons.title: Securing Outbound and East-West Traffic
lessons.summary: Network Firewall, Gateway Load Balancer, proxies and centralized inspection.
takeaways: Network Firewall has stateless then stateful engines, domain and Suricata rules, endpoints per AZ in dedicated subnets, and logs to S3/CloudWatch/Firehose.
Inspection only works if routing sends traffic through the endpoint and keeps it symmetric.
Choose distributed, centralized egress or centralized inspection by cost, control and latency trade-offs.
GWLB with GENEVE scales third-party appliances; endpoint policies and DNS Firewall add egress control.

lessons.title: Security Groups, NACLs, Firewall Manager and Auditing
lessons.summary: Inter-VPC controls and a network audit strategy across accounts.
takeaways: Use security groups (stateful, SG references) for micro-segmentation; NACLs (stateless) for coarse guardrails; endpoint policies for service-level egress control.
Firewall Manager enforces WAF, Shield, SG, Network Firewall, DNS Firewall and NACL policies across an organization using Config.
An audit strategy combines CloudTrail, Config, flow/DNS/LB/edge/WAF logs, centralized storage and automated alarms.
Correlate sources by IP, instance and time; retain in a protected log archive account.

lessons.title: Encryption in Transit and Certificate Management
lessons.summary: IPsec, MACsec, TLS, ACM and Private CA under the shared responsibility model.
takeaways: Name the encryption control for every segment: TLS at edge and origin, IPsec/MACsec on hybrid links, Nitro and TLS inside, TLS to AWS services.
Direct Connect is private but not encrypted; add MACsec (hop) or IPsec (end-to-end tunnel).
ACM issues free public certificates with DNS validation and auto-renewal; CloudFront needs us-east-1; Private CA covers internal and exportable certificates.
AWS provides the capability; you configure and enforce encryption, certificates and policies.
